  • Liberace, the pianist who performed in outfits encrusted with rhinestones and feathers, surrounded by candelabras, playing pop songs in an operatic style — his entire persona was campy. Nobody else played piano like a Vegas showgirl, and he did it with complete commitment.
  • Old soap operas where characters gasp dramatically, swoon onto sofas, and receive devastating news while an orchestra swells beneath them — accidentally campy. The intent was emotion; the result is unintentional comedy.
  • A Halloween costume of a vampire where someone wears a dramatic black cape, drawn-on widow's peak, full pale face paint, plastic fangs, and speaks in an exaggerated Transylvanian accent all night — that's campy. They took a concept and pushed every element to the extreme.
  • Certain superhero films that don't take themselves seriously — where the villain has an absurdly theatrical monologue, the costumes are gloriously impractical, and the whole film seems to be winking at you — are often described as campy.

This is the most important thing to understand about "campy": it's said with warmth.

When someone says "that movie is so campy," they often mean it with genuine delight — not contempt. Camp is something people can love. The word acknowledges that something is over-the-top and artificial, but frames that as a feature, not a flaw.

This is what separates campy from just being bad. A bad film fails at what it's trying to do and offers nothing. A campy film may also fail at realism or subtlety, but it succeeds at delivering theatrical, exaggerated energy that becomes its own kind of entertainment. The spirit and commitment — whether earnest or knowing — give it charm.

You can say "I love this show, it's so campy" and genuinely mean it as a compliment.

Cheesy: Something cheesy is cheap, low-quality, or unsophisticated — and the result is usually a little cringe-worthy. It lacks the theatrical exaggeration and playfulness of camp. A cheesy joke is just a bad, corny joke. A campy scene is an gloriously overdramatic one.

Corny: Old-fashioned, overly sentimental, and outdated in a naïve way. Corn is more about sincere, wholesome sentimentality gone wrong. It doesn't have the theatrical flamboyance of camp.

Melodramatic: Exaggerated emotional reactions — crying at small things, reacting to everything like it's a tragedy. Melodrama is one ingredient of campy, but "campy" is much broader. It includes costumes, aesthetics, dialogue, set design, personality — the whole presentation.

Kitsch: Refers to objects or art of poor or garish taste that have an ironic or nostalgic charm (a plastic flamingo on a lawn, a velvet Elvis painting). Kitsch is about things; campy is more about performance, behavior, and the spirit of presentation.

Theatrical: Performative and dramatic. "Theatrical" is a neutral or even positive word — great stage actors are theatrical. "Campy" adds the specific quality of excess and artificial over-the-top-ness. All campy things are theatrical, but not all theatrical things are campy.

Flamboyant: Means strikingly bold, showy, or colorful in personality or appearance. Flamboyant can describe camp, but it's a milder, more general word. Something flamboyant is attention-grabbing; something campy is attention-grabbing and theatrically excessive in a way that feels knowingly artificial.

"Campy" is deeply associated with LGBTQ+ culture — particularly gay culture and drag performance — where theatrical self-expression, playing with gender and identity, and embracing what mainstream culture called "too much" became a celebrated art form. The sensibility of camp was, for a long time, a coded language and a form of self-expression for queer people: finding joy and humor in performance, artifice, and excess.

Many of the most iconic examples of camp come from this world: drag queens, queer nightlife, certain films with large gay followings. However, "campy" is now a mainstream English word used across all contexts — film criticism, fashion, home decor, music, sports commentary, and describing people's personalities. You don't need any LGBTQ+ connection to use or understand it today, but knowing its roots helps you understand why it carries such an affectionate, celebratory spirit.

• "I love that horror movie — yes, it's campy, but that's exactly why it's fun to watch."
  • "The villain's costume was so campy: a purple cape, a monocle, and a mustache he kept twirling."
  • "She threw a campy birthday party with pink flamingos, glitter everywhere, and a disco ball over the cake table."
  • "His performance was deliberately campy — he played every scene with maximum theatrical flair, and it worked beautifully."
  • "The film was supposed to be a serious thriller, but the acting was so over-the-top that it ended up being accidentally campy."

If you had to remember just one thing: campy = theatrical, exaggerated, and artificial in a way that's deliberately over-the-top and often lovably so. It's excess as entertainment, performed with flair.
2466:
A canal is an artificial waterway — a long, narrow channel that humans dig into the ground and fill with water. The single most important thing to remember about a canal is that it is man-made, not natural. That's what separates it from a river or a stream, which form on their own through natural processes. A canal exists because people planned it, designed it, and built it for a specific purpose.

Think of it this way: a river is nature's water highway; a canal is humanity's water highway.

A canal is typically long and narrow, with relatively straight or gently curving sides. Unlike a winding river with uneven banks, a canal usually has clean, engineered walls — often made of stone, concrete, or compacted earth. It has a flat, measured bottom and a controlled water level. It looks deliberate, because it is deliberate.

Canals are built for three main purposes:

1. Transportation (Navigation canals)
Before roads and railways, moving heavy goods overland was slow and exhausting. Canals solved this by giving boats a smooth, calm waterway to travel through land that would otherwise be impassable by water.

The most famous examples in the world are:

  • The Suez Canal (Egypt) — a massive canal cutting through Egypt that connects the Mediterranean Sea to the Red Sea. Without it, ships would have to sail all the way around the entire continent of Africa to get from Europe to Asia.
  • The Panama Canal (Panama) — connects the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean through the narrow strip of land in Central America. Before it existed, ships had to sail around the stormy tip of South America — a journey of thousands of extra miles.
  • The canals of Venice, Italy — Venice is a city built on islands, and its canals are its streets. Instead of driving cars, people travel by boat through a network of canals.

In England, during the 18th and 19th centuries, an entire network of canals was built to carry coal, pottery, and goods between factories and cities. These were called narrowboats canals because the boats that used them were long and very narrow to fit the channels.

2. Irrigation canals
Farmers have used canals for thousands of years to bring water from rivers and lakes to their fields. An irrigation canal is essentially a network of water channels that branches out across farmland like veins, directing water exactly where crops need it. Ancient civilizations in Egypt, Mesopotamia (modern-day Iraq), and India built massive irrigation canal systems that allowed entire populations to survive and thrive in otherwise dry regions.

3. Drainage canals
Sometimes the problem is too much water. Low-lying areas, swamps, or flood-prone land can be made usable by digging canals that carry excess water away. The Netherlands, for example, is famous for using canals (and other engineering) to drain large areas of land that were once under the sea, turning them into livable, farmable territory.
How boats travel uphill through canals: Locks

Here's something fascinating that many learners don't know: canals aren't always flat. Land rises and falls, but water doesn't flow uphill on its own. So how do canal boats cross a hill?

The answer is a device called a lock. A lock is a gated chamber built into the canal. When a boat needs to go uphill, it enters the lock, the gates close behind it, and water is pumped into the chamber, raising the water level (and the boat) until it matches the higher section of the canal ahead. The front gates then open, and the boat floats forward at the new, higher level. Going downhill works in reverse — water is let out of the chamber to lower the boat. Locks are one of the cleverest pieces of engineering in history, and you'll find them on almost any canal that crosses uneven terrain.

The word "canal" is also widely used in medicine and biology to describe any narrow, tube-like passage inside the body. The logic is the same — it's a channel that carries something from one place to another. Here are the most common ones you'll encounter:

  • Ear canal — the narrow passage in your ear that leads from the outer ear to the eardrum. Sound travels through it like a boat through a canal.
  • Birth canal — the passage (the vagina and cervix) through which a baby travels when being born.
  • Root canal — the hollow channel running through the root of a tooth, containing nerves and blood vessels. When dentists perform a "root canal procedure," they are cleaning out this channel.
  • Alimentary canal — the entire digestive tube running from your mouth, through your stomach and intestines, to your anus. Everything you eat travels through it.
  • Spinal canal — the tunnel inside your backbone (vertebral column) through which your spinal cord runs.

In all these cases, the idea is identical: a enclosed, tube-like path through which something moves.
Canals vs. rivers vs. streams — a clear distinction

Since these words are often confused, here's how they relate:

  • A river is a large, natural flow of water moving across land toward a sea, lake, or another river. Nobody built it.
  • A stream (or creek) is a smaller, natural flow of water. Same idea as a river, just smaller.
  • A canal is always artificial. Someone built it. It doesn't exist without human effort.

There are cases where canals follow or are built alongside natural waterways, but the canal itself — its walls, its controlled depth, its designed route — is always a human creation.

Canal = an artificial water channel built by humans. It can be enormous (connecting two oceans) or small (watering a field), it can be a waterway for ships or a passage inside your body — but the common thread is always a purposefully constructed channel through which water, boats, sound, or biological material travels. It is planned, built, and shaped by intelligent design rather than by nature.
2467: A canapé is a tiny, bite-sized piece of food made up of two essential parts: a small, firm base and a topping placed on it. That's the heart of it. Think of it like a miniature open-faced sandwich — except it is far smaller, more refined, and is never a meal by itself.

1. The base
The base is a small, firm, flat piece of food that acts as a little platform. It needs to be sturdy enough to hold the topping without falling apart. Common bases include:

  • A small piece of toasted bread or a toast round
  • A cracker
  • A small pastry shell
  • A slice of cucumber or a similar vegetable used as an edible platform

The base is almost always just one or two bites in size. You pick it up with your fingers, not with a fork or knife.

2. The topping
The topping sits on the base and is the "flavourful" part. It is almost always savoury (not sweet). Common toppings include:

  • Smoked salmon or other fish
  • Shrimp or prawns
  • Cream cheese or soft cheese
  • Liver pâté (a smooth, spreadable meat paste)
  • Caviar (fish eggs, often considered a luxury topping)
  • Cured meats like ham or salami
  • Vegetables with a dip or spread

Sometimes a tiny garnish — a sprig of herb, a thin slice of lemon, a dot of sauce — is placed on top of the topping to make the canapé look elegant.

A canapé is not a dish you sit down to eat as a meal. It belongs to a specific social context: parties, receptions, cocktail hours, and formal gatherings. When guests arrive and are standing around with drinks in their hands, a waiter or host often moves around with a tray full of canapés. Guests pick one up, pop it in their mouth, and carry on with their conversation. The whole idea is that it is small enough to eat cleanly and quickly — in one bite, ideally — without needing a plate, cutlery, or any fuss.

Because of this role, canapés are also called finger food and they fall under the broader category of hors d'oeuvres (small appetisers served before a main meal or as standalone party food).
Key Qualities That Define a Canapé

• Small: Always bite-sized. If you need more than two bites, it is not really a canapé.
  • Structured: It always has a base. This is what separates a canapé from, say, a simple cheese cube on a toothpick — a canapé has a foundation.
  • Open-faced: There is no second layer of bread or covering on top. The topping is exposed.
  • Savoury: Almost always savoury, not sweet.
  • Elegant and presented: Canapés are known for being neatly assembled and visually attractive. They are associated with upscale or formal occasions, though they appear at casual parties too.
  • Finger food: Meant to be picked up and eaten by hand, without utensils.
How It Differs From Similar Things

• A sandwich is much larger, has bread on two sides, and is a meal or snack in itself. A canapé is open-faced and too small to be a meal.
  • A bruschetta (grilled bread with toppings) is similar in structure, but it is bigger and is considered a starter dish you eat while seated, not a one-bite party item.
  • A cracker with cheese could technically become a canapé if assembled carefully with a topping and served on a party tray, but the word "canapé" implies a deliberate, neat construction — it is prepared with care and intention, not just casually placed together.

A canapé is a small, neat, one-bite piece of finger food with a firm edible base (like toast or a cracker) topped with something savoury (like fish, cheese, or meat). It is specifically designed for social events where people eat standing up, holding a drink. It is elegant, carefully assembled, and meant to be eaten in a single bite without any utensils.
2468:
A canard is a false story or claim — one that is made up, has no solid basis in fact, and yet gets repeated and spread around as if it were true.

Think of it as a lie that travels. Not just a private lie told to one person, but a false idea that circulates publicly — in the news, in politics, in everyday conversation — and takes on a life of its own. The key thing about a canard is that people keep repeating it, often without checking if it's actually true.
What Makes a Canard Different from Just "a Lie"

This is important, because canard is a more specific and precise word than simply "a lie" or "a false statement."

Here's how to think about it:

  • A lie is any false statement, even something said once to one person.
  • A rumor is unverified information — it might be true or false; nobody knows for sure yet.
  • A canard is a false story that is already in circulation and being treated as fact even though it isn't. The falseness is often known (or should be known), yet the story keeps spreading anyway.

A canard is also typically more specific than a general myth. It tends to be a particular claim — something pointed, often used to mislead or manipulate — rather than a vague cultural belief.

Some more nuances worth knowing:

  • A canard can be started deliberately (to mislead someone) or can arise accidentally and just never get corrected.
  • It is most commonly used in serious, formal contexts — journalism, politics, debate, academic writing. You'd be more likely to read "that's a tired old canard" in a newspaper editorial than hear it in casual conversation.
  • It often carries a slightly contemptuous tone, as if to say: "This claim is not just wrong — it's embarrassingly wrong, and people really should know better by now."
Common Situations Where You'll See It Used

In politics: Politicians often accuse their opponents of spreading canards — false claims designed to damage their reputation or mislead the public.

"The allegation that she raised taxes on the middle class is a canard — the record clearly shows the opposite."

In media and journalism: Journalists use it when debunking a widely repeated false claim.

"The idea that sugar makes children hyperactive is a popular canard that science has repeatedly debunked."

In debate or argument: When someone wants to dismiss a false premise that keeps getting brought up.

"We've heard this canard before, and it doesn't hold up to scrutiny."

Notice in these examples that the word often appears with words like "old," "tired," "familiar," "persistent," or "popular." This reflects the key quality of a canard — it's a falsehood with staying power.

In the world of aircraft and aeronautics, canard has a completely different and unrelated meaning.

A canard refers to a small horizontal wing or fin placed at the front of an aircraft, near the nose — ahead of the main wings. This is the opposite of the traditional aircraft design, where stabilizers sit at the tail. The canard wing helps with lift and control.

Several modern fighter jets (like the Eurofighter Typhoon) and some civilian planes use this design, called a canard configuration.

This is a technical term used specifically by pilots, engineers, and aviation enthusiasts. In everyday language, if someone says "canard" without any aviation context, they almost always mean the first meaning — the false story.

What it isA false story or claim that circulates publicly as if it were true
Key qualityIt spreads and persists — it's not just a one-off lie
ToneFormal, slightly contemptuous toward those repeating the falsehood
Where you'll see itPolitics, journalism, formal debate
Second meaningA forward-facing wing on an aircraft (aviation only)
One Last Thing: How to Use It Yourself

If you want to use "canard" in your own writing or speech, use it when:

  1. A specific false claim exists (not just a vague untruth).
  2. That claim has been repeated or spread — it's "out there."
  3. You want to clearly label it as false and perhaps express that it's frustrating or tiresome that people still believe it.

Avoid using it as a fancy synonym for just any lie or mistake. Save it for the persistent, circulating, false-claim type of situation — that's where it earns its precision.
2469:
Cancerous means relating to, characteristic of, or affected by cancer.

To understand this fully, you first need a clear picture of what cancer is.

In your body, trillions of cells are constantly growing, dividing, and dying in a perfectly organised way. Your body controls this process tightly — telling cells when to grow, when to stop, and when to die. Cancer is what happens when this control breaks down. Some cells start dividing and multiplying without stopping, ignoring the body's signals. They pile up, invade nearby tissues, and can spread to distant parts of the body through the blood or lymph system. The damage they cause can eventually threaten life.

When something is described as cancerous, it means it has this quality — it behaves like cancer, or it belongs to cancer, or it is caused by cancer.

1. Cancerous cells
These are cells that have undergone abnormal changes and no longer follow the body's rules. They divide uncontrollably, do not respond to stop signals, and do not die when they are supposed to. They are the building blocks of cancer.

2. A cancerous tumour (or cancerous growth)
A tumour is simply a lump or mass of cells. Not all tumours are dangerous — a benign (non-cancerous) tumour grows slowly, stays in one place, and does not invade surrounding tissue. A cancerous tumour (also called a malignant tumour) is the opposite — it grows aggressively, invades neighbouring tissue, and can spread to other parts of the body. This spreading process is called metastasis.

3. A cancerous tissue
If a doctor says a tissue sample is cancerous, it means the tissue contains cells that are malignant — abnormal and potentially life-threatening.

4. A cancerous condition / a cancerous disease
This means a disease that is driven by cancer, or a medical state characterised by the presence of cancer.
The Key Qualities That Make Something "Cancerous"

When something is cancerous, it has some or all of these characteristics:

  • Uncontrolled growth — it multiplies without stopping
  • Invasion — it spreads into and damages surrounding, healthy areas
  • Resistance to correction — the normal checks and balances that would stop it have failed
  • Destructive potential — if left unchecked, it causes serious, possibly irreversible harm
An Important Distinction: Cancerous vs. Benign

These two words are often paired in medical conversations, and understanding the contrast sharpens your grasp of "cancerous."

  • Benign = not cancerous. A benign growth stays localised, does not invade other tissues, and is rarely life-threatening.
  • Cancerous (malignant) = dangerous. It grows aggressively, invades, spreads, and destroys.

So when a doctor says, "The biopsy results show the tumour is cancerous," it means the tumour is malignant — not just a harmless lump, but a dangerous, invasive growth.

You will sometimes see the word pre-cancerous (also written as precancerous). This means something that is not yet cancerous but shows abnormal changes that could develop into cancer if left untreated. Think of it as an early warning stage — the cells are abnormal, but have not yet become fully malignant. Doctors try to catch and treat pre-cancerous conditions precisely to prevent them from becoming cancerous.

"Cancerous" is also used powerfully as a metaphor outside medicine. In this figurative sense, it describes anything that:

  • spreads gradually and silently
  • corrupts or destroys from within
  • is hard to stop once it takes hold
  • weakens or ruins whatever it touches

This use borrows the qualities of cancer — its insidious spread, its destructive nature — and applies them to social, moral, or organisational situations.

Examples:

  • "Corruption is a cancerous force in any society — it starts small, spreads quietly, and eventually hollows out everything."
  • "The manager's toxic attitude was cancerous to team morale."
  • "Misinformation, left unchecked, becomes cancerous to public trust."
  • "The bitterness between the two factions was cancerous — it infected every decision the organisation made."

In all these cases, the speaker is saying: this problem behaves exactly like cancer does in a body. It grows, it spreads, it harms, and if you don't act, it destroys.

ContextWhat "cancerous" means
MedicalRelating to or affected by cancer; malignant; characterised by uncontrolled, invasive cell growth
FigurativeSpreading harmfully from within; corrupting or destroying gradually and insidiously

One-line definition you can carry with you:
Cancerous means relating to cancer (in medicine) or, more broadly, anything that grows, spreads, and causes destruction in the way cancer does.
Putting It All Together: Example Sentences

1. The surgeon confirmed that the lump was cancerous and recommended immediate treatment.
  2. Early screening can detect cancerous changes in cells before they spread.
  3. Not all tumours are cancerous — some are completely benign.
  4. The pre-cancerous lesion was removed before it could develop into a full-blown cancer.
  5. Jealousy, when nurtured, becomes cancerous — it eats away at relationships quietly.
  6. The toxic company culture had grown cancerous, driving away the best employees one by one.
2470:
When someone is candid, they tell you the truth openly and directly — even when that truth is uncomfortable, awkward, or not what you want to hear. A candid person doesn't sugarcoat things, doesn't hide their real opinions, and doesn't say one thing while thinking another. What they say on the outside matches exactly what they think on the inside.

Think of it this way: if you ask a friend "Does this outfit look bad?" and they say "Honestly, yes, it doesn't suit you" — that friend is being candid.

Being candid has two key ingredients working together:

1. Honesty — You say what is actually true, not what is convenient or flattering.

2. Openness — You don't hold back or hide your real thoughts. You share them freely and directly.

Remove either ingredient, and you're no longer truly candid. Someone who is honest but stays silent isn't being candid. Someone who speaks up but twists the truth isn't being candid either. Candid means both — speaking up and being truthful.

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Candid ≠ Rude or cruel.
A candid person isn't trying to hurt you. Their directness comes from a place of respect or care, not from a desire to insult. The goal is truth, not pain.

Candid ≠ Blunt.
"Blunt" means direct to the point of being harsh or tactless — no concern for your feelings whatsoever. Candid has a softer quality. A candid person can still be kind and considerate in how they deliver the truth, even though they don't hide the truth itself.

Candid ≠ Outspoken.
An outspoken person loudly and publicly expresses their opinions, sometimes even on topics no one asked about. A candid person simply responds truthfully and openly when speaking — it's about the quality of their honesty, not the boldness or volume of their personality.
A Very Common Use: Asking to "Be Candid"

In everyday conversation, you'll often hear phrases like:

  • "Can I be candid with you?"
  • "Let me be completely candid."
  • "To be candid…"

These phrases are a polite way of signaling: "I'm about to say something honest that you might not love hearing, but I mean well." It's almost like a warning and a sign of respect at the same time — the speaker is telling you that what follows will be the genuine truth, not a polished or softened version of it.

• "Her candid feedback helped me improve my writing more than any polite comment ever did."
  • "The CEO gave a surprisingly candid interview, admitting the company had made serious mistakes."
  • "He was candid about his fears, which made others feel comfortable opening up too."
  • "In a candid moment, she confessed she didn't actually enjoy her job."
  • "I'll be candid — I don't think this plan will work."

"Candid" also describes a photograph (or video) taken of someone naturally and spontaneously — when they are unaware of the camera, not posing, and just being themselves in the moment.

A candid photo captures real, unguarded human moments: a genuine laugh, a look of surprise, a quiet, thoughtful expression. It is the opposite of a staged or posed photo.

This meaning connects perfectly to the core idea of the word: just as a candid person shows you who they really are without putting on a performance, a candid photo shows you who a person really is without them putting on a pose.

When someone describes a person, a conversation, or an interview as "candid," there's usually a sense of refreshingness about it. In a world where people often carefully choose their words to protect themselves or please others, candid honesty stands out. It feels rare, trustworthy, and even courageous.

That's why you'll often see phrases like "refreshingly candid" or "surprisingly candid" — because true candor is something people genuinely appreciate and notice.

Candid = honest + open + direct, without hiding or softening the truth — but without being cruel either.

If someone calls you candid, take it as a compliment. It means people trust that what you say is what you really think — and that is a rare and valued quality.
2471:
A candidate is a person who is being considered or evaluated for something — a job, a position, an award, an exam, or any kind of selection process. The word captures a specific moment in time: the person is in the running, but has not yet been chosen (or rejected).

Think of it this way: a candidate stands at a crossroads. They have entered a process, and someone — a committee, voters, an employer, an examiner — will decide their fate. That state of "being considered" is the heart of what a candidate is.

1. Jobs and Careers

When a company advertises a job and people apply, those applicants become candidates. A hiring manager reviews their resumes, calls them for interviews, and evaluates them. Until a final decision is made, each person being considered is a candidate.

"We interviewed five candidates for the marketing role."
"She was the strongest candidate we had seen all year."

Notice: once someone is hired, they stop being a candidate and become an employee. The word only applies during the selection phase.

2. Politics and Elections

In politics, a candidate is someone who is competing in an election — trying to win votes and get elected to a position like president, prime minister, mayor, or member of parliament.

"Three candidates are running for governor."
"The candidate gave a speech at the town hall."

Here, the "selection process" is the election itself, and the "selectors" are the voters. A political candidate campaigns, debates, and makes promises — all to convince people to choose them.

3. Exams and Academic Qualifications

In academic settings, a person sitting for a formal examination is called a candidate. This is especially common in British English.

"All candidates must arrive thirty minutes before the exam."
"PhD candidates are required to defend their thesis."

In this use, the "selection process" is the exam or evaluation, and the outcome is whether they pass or receive a qualification.

While the word most often refers to people, it can also describe things that are being considered for a particular outcome. This is a natural extension of the same idea.

"This old building is a candidate for demolition."
"Given his poor diet and stress levels, he's a candidate for heart disease."

In these cases, the word signals that something has the qualities that make it likely to be chosen for — or lead to — a particular result.
What Makes Someone a "Candidate" vs. Just a "Person"?

The word carries specific weight. Not everyone interested in a job is a candidate — only those who have formally entered the consideration process. Not everyone who could run for office is a candidate — only those who have declared their intention and are actively competing.

So "candidate" implies:

  • Intentionality — they have put themselves forward, or been put forward by others
  • A formal process — there is some evaluation or selection happening
  • Uncertainty — the outcome has not yet been decided
  • Competition or standards — they are being measured against others or against a benchmark

• "Leading candidate" — the person most likely to be chosen at a given moment
  • "Ideal candidate" — the perfect person for the role, often used in job postings
  • "Strong/weak candidate" — describes how well-suited someone is
  • "Shortlisted candidate" — someone who has passed initial screening and made it to the final group being considered
  • "Candidate for [something negative]" — used informally to mean someone is at risk of a bad outcome ("He's a candidate for burnout if he keeps working like this.")
The Subtle Emotion of the Word

"Candidate" is a neutral, professional word, but it quietly carries tension. It suggests that something is at stake — a person's career, a country's leadership, a student's future. Whenever you see it, something is being evaluated, and a decision is coming.

A candidate is a person (or thing) that is officially in the running to be selected, chosen, or evaluated for a position, role, award, or outcome — someone who is being considered, but whose fate has not yet been decided.
2472:
Candor is the quality of being genuinely open and honest in what you say, especially when the truth is difficult, uncomfortable, or sensitive. A person who speaks with candor tells you what they truly think — plainly, sincerely, and without hiding behind vague or diplomatic language.

Think of it this way: if your friend shows you a painting they worked on for weeks, and it's honestly not very good, most people would say something polite and non-committal like "it's interesting!" But a person with candor would say, warmly but honestly, "I think the colors clash a bit — maybe try reworking the background?" That is candor. They told you the truth because they respect you enough to do so.

Candor has three key ingredients working together:

Honesty. The person is not lying, exaggerating, or hiding the truth. What they say reflects what they actually believe or know.

Directness. They don't beat around the bush. They say what needs to be said clearly, without burying it in so many soft words that the message gets lost.

Sincerity. Candor comes from a place of genuine goodwill. It is not about shocking someone or being harsh for its own sake. The honest words are spoken because the person truly wants to help, inform, or connect.

All three work together. Honesty without directness is vagueness. Directness without sincerity is rudeness. Candor is the combination of all three — truth, delivered clearly, with good intent.

Candor often requires a quiet kind of courage. Many people avoid saying difficult truths because they fear hurting feelings, causing conflict, or being judged. A person who speaks with candor has decided that honesty — delivered kindly — is more respectful and more valuable than comfortable silence or false reassurance.

This is why candor is generally admired. When someone is candid with you, it feels like a form of respect. They trust you enough to handle the truth, and they care enough about you to give it to you.

Candor tends to appear in situations where honesty about something difficult or sensitive is notable or admirable:

  • A doctor speaks with candor about a patient's diagnosis, explaining exactly what the illness means rather than softening it into meaninglessness.
  • A manager shows candor in a performance review, clearly telling an employee what they need to improve rather than giving only generic praise.
  • A public figure is praised for their candor in an interview where they openly discussed their personal struggles.
  • A friend's candor is appreciated when they honestly say they didn't enjoy the movie instead of pretending they did.

You'll also see the phrase "with candor" very commonly — it means "in an open and honest manner." And the phrase "refreshing candor" is used when someone's honesty comes as a pleasant surprise, especially in situations where people usually dodge the truth.

Because candor involves being honest and direct, people sometimes confuse it with negative things. Here's what it is not:

Candor is not harshness. A harsh person says difficult things without caring about the impact. A candid person says difficult things while caring about the impact. The goal is truth, not pain.

Candor is not rudeness. Rudeness is dismissive or disrespectful. Candor is respectful — it takes the other person seriously.

Candor is not oversharing. Telling strangers personal details about your life is not candor. Candor is about honesty and openness in what you do choose to say, not about saying everything you think at all times.

Candor is not criticism for its own sake. Someone who picks apart everything just to seem smart or superior is not demonstrating candor. Candor has a constructive, sincere motive behind it.
How Candor Differs from Similar Words

Several words are close in meaning to candor, but each has a slightly different shade:

Honesty is the broadest of these words — it simply means not lying or deceiving. Candor goes a step further by implying that you are also open and forthcoming, not just technically truthful but actively sharing what is real.

Frankness is very close to candor and the two are often interchangeable. However, frankness can sometimes carry a slightly blunter edge — a frank person might tell you something directly with little cushioning. Candor tends to carry a slightly warmer tone, suggesting that the honesty is offered with goodwill.

Transparency usually refers to openness about processes, decisions, intentions, or information — often used for organizations, governments, or systems ("the company needs more transparency"). Candor is more personal and conversational — it's about how an individual speaks.

Sincerity is about being genuine in your feelings and intentions, not fake or performative. Candor includes sincerity but is specifically about the act of speaking honestly, not just feeling genuine inside.

Here are examples showing how the word is used naturally:

  • "I admired her candor when she told me, honestly, that my business idea had a serious flaw."
  • "He spoke with rare candor about the mistakes he made early in his career."
  • "The coach's candor was sometimes uncomfortable, but the players knew it made them better."
  • "What I appreciated most about the interview was her candor — she didn't give rehearsed, polished answers."
  • "He looked me in the eye and, with complete candor, said he didn't think the project was ready."

The word candor is part of a small family of related words you'll often encounter:

Candid (adjective) — used to describe a person, remark, or moment that shows candor. "She gave me a candid opinion." / "He was surprisingly candid about his fears."

Candidly (adverb) — in a candid manner. "Candidly, I don't think this plan will work." / "She spoke candidly about her experience."

When you see any of these forms, the core idea is always the same: honest, open, direct, and sincere.

Candor is valued precisely because it is rare. In everyday life, people often soften, hide, or avoid the truth to keep the peace, protect feelings, or make themselves look good. Candor is the deliberate choice to cut through that and speak plainly.

This makes candor a cornerstone of real trust. In friendships, workplaces, leadership, and relationships, the people and environments where candor is practiced tend to be healthier, more effective, and more trustworthy — because everyone knows they will get the truth, not a comfortable version of it.

In short: candor is honest speech delivered with sincerity and goodwill. It is the opposite of evasion, flattery, and comfortable half-truths.
2473: The word canine has two distinct meanings when used as a noun. Both are common, so you need to know both to fully understand this word.

A canine is any animal that belongs to the biological family Canidae. This family includes:

  • Domestic dogs (the most common meaning in everyday speech)
  • Wolves
  • Foxes
  • Jackals
  • Coyotes
  • Dingoes

All of these animals are canines. They share common features: four legs, a snout, sharp teeth, claws, and fur. Most of them are predators or scavengers.

In everyday conversation, when someone says "canine," they almost always mean a dog specifically. It's simply a more formal or technical word for a dog. You'll often hear it used by veterinarians, scientists, police officers, and military personnel.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The veterinarian specializes in treating canines."
  • "The police deployed a canine to track the suspect." (Here, "canine" refers to a trained police dog.)
  • "Wolves are wild canines."

Note: You may have seen the term K-9, especially in the context of police dogs. "K-9" is simply a phonetic shorthand for "canine" — the letter K sounds like "kay" and 9 sounds like "nine," making "K-9" sound like "canine." So a "K-9 unit" in a police force is a unit that uses trained dogs.

A canine (also called a canine tooth) is a specific type of tooth found in humans and many other mammals.

You have four canines in your mouth:

  • One in the upper left side
  • One in the upper right side
  • One in the lower left side
  • One in the lower right side

Where exactly are they?

If you count your teeth starting from the very center of your mouth and going outward, the order is:

  1. Incisors — the flat front teeth (used for biting)
  2. Canines — the sharp, pointed teeth right next to the incisors
  3. Premolars — further back
  4. Molars — the large, flat teeth at the back

So the canines sit at the corners of your mouth, between your front teeth and your back teeth.

What do they look like?

Canines are taller and more pointed than the other teeth around them. Their tip comes to a single sharp point, almost like a fang. This pointy shape is their most defining feature.

What are they used for?

Canines are designed for gripping and tearing food — especially tough or chewy food like meat. While your front incisors cut food and your back molars grind it, your canines help you grip and rip it apart.

Why are they called "canines"?

The name comes from the connection to dogs (canines). Dogs — and other members of the canine family — have very prominent, large, fang-like teeth. Since these pointed teeth in humans resemble a dog's fangs, they were named after the canine animal.

Examples in sentences:

  • "The dentist told me my upper left canine has a small cavity."
  • "Humans have four canines in total."
  • "He bared his canines in an aggressive snarl." (often used dramatically or metaphorically)

Other names for this tooth

The canine tooth also goes by a couple of other names you might encounter:

  • "Eye tooth" — This is an informal, old-fashioned name specifically for the upper canines. The name comes from the belief (historically) that these teeth were positioned beneath the eyes. You'll mostly hear this in older writing or from older speakers.
  • "Fang" — This is not a precise dental term, but in everyday language (and in fiction — think vampires or werewolves), the word "fang" refers to a long, sharp canine tooth.
How to Tell Which Meaning is Intended

Since "canine" has two noun meanings, context will almost always make it clear:

  • If the sentence is about animals, pets, dogs, police work, or veterinary care → it means a dog or member of the dog family.
  • If the sentence is about teeth, dentistry, the mouth, or biting → it means a pointed tooth.

Meaning
Canine (animal)A dog or any related animal (wolf, fox, coyote, etc.)
Canine (tooth)The four sharp, pointed teeth in the corners of your mouth

Both meanings are connected by the same idea: dogs. One refers to the animal itself; the other refers to a tooth that resembles a dog's fang.
2474:
A canister is a rigid, cylindrical container — round like a tube or a drum — that has a removable lid or cover. It is designed to store, hold, or carry something safely inside, whether that something is a solid, a powder, a liquid, or a gas.

The key qualities that define a canister:

  • It is solid and hard (not floppy like a bag or flexible like a pouch)
  • It has a removable top (unlike a sealed food can that needs a can opener)
  • It is typically round/cylindrical in shape (unlike a box, which has flat sides)
  • It is compact enough to carry — you can usually hold one in your hand

This is why a cardboard box is not a canister, a glass bottle with a narrow neck is not a canister, and a plastic zip-lock bag is not a canister.

1. Kitchen / storage canisters
These are the round containers you often see sitting on kitchen counters, used to store dry goods like flour, sugar, coffee, tea, or rice. They usually come in matching sets and keep the contents fresh by sealing out air and moisture.

2. Gas canisters
A pressurized metal container that holds gas. You see these in several situations:

  • Camping gas canisters — small metal cylinders you screw onto a portable stove to cook outdoors
  • Aerosol canisters — the cylindrical metal body of products like spray paint or deodorant; the canister holds the product under pressure and releases it when you press the nozzle
  • Tear gas canisters — metal cylinders fired or thrown by police/security forces that release a cloud of irritant gas to disperse a crowd

3. Film canisters
Small cylindrical plastic or metal containers that held rolls of photographic film — the film used in cameras before the age of smartphones and digital photography. They were very common in the 20th century. Even after the film was removed, people often repurposed empty film canisters to store tiny items like coins, pills, or pins, because they closed so neatly.

4. Filter canisters
Cylindrical units that clean or purify something passing through them:

  • A gas mask canister is the round cartridge screwed onto the side or front of the mask; it filters out toxic chemicals or particles from the air before the wearer breathes it in
  • A canister vacuum cleaner is a type of vacuum cleaner where the main body — the cylindrical unit housing the motor and dust collection — is called the canister; it's separate from the hose and cleaning head

5. Military canisters
Historically, canister shot was a devastating weapon fired from cannons: a metal canister packed with dozens of small iron balls, which scattered in all directions like a giant shotgun blast upon firing. Today, the word is also used for sealed containers that store and even launch certain missiles or rockets — the weapon stays protected inside the canister until it's fired.

6. Smoke / signal canisters
Used by the military, emergency services, and outdoor enthusiasts. When activated, these release a thick cloud of colored smoke — used to signal a location, mark a landing zone for helicopters, or create a visual screen during military operations.

No matter which canister you're talking about — kitchen, gas, film, military, filter, or smoke — they all share the same fundamental idea: a rigid, cylindrical, enclosed container with a sealed or closeable end, used to hold something safely inside.

The word almost always implies something practical and sturdy. A canister is not decorative by nature — it exists to contain, protect, or dispense something.

• "She pried open the canister of ground coffee and filled the machine."
  • "The police threw a tear gas canister to break up the protest."
  • "He found an old film canister in the back of the drawer."
  • "Screw the gas canister onto the stove before you strike the lighter."
  • "The soldier pulled the pin on the smoke canister and tossed it into the field to mark their position."
  • "The gas mask's filter canister needs to be replaced every few months."

In short: whenever you see or hear the word canister, picture a sturdy, round container with a lid — something built to hold its contents securely, whether on a kitchen shelf or in a battlefield.
2475:
A canker is a destructive sore, wound, or area of decay that eats into living tissue — and crucially, it doesn't stay put. It tends to spread, grow worse, and damage more than just the spot where it started. Think of it as a kind of rot that creeps.

The word appears in several different contexts — human health, plants, animals, and even as a metaphor — but this central idea of a spreading, destructive wound or decay runs through all of them.
1. In the Human Body — The Canker Sore

The most everyday meaning you'll encounter is a canker sore: a small, painful ulcer that forms inside the mouth — on the inner lip, cheek, tongue, or the soft tissue of the gums.

Canker sores are:

  • Shallow and round, with a white or yellowish centre and a red border
  • Not on the outside of the lips (that's a cold sore, which is different — caused by a virus and contagious; canker sores are neither)
  • Painful out of proportion to their size — even a tiny one can sting sharply when eating, drinking, or speaking
  • Self-healing — they usually disappear on their own within one to two weeks

When someone says "I have a canker," they almost certainly mean one of these mouth sores.
2. In Plants and Trees — Plant Canker

In botany and gardening, a canker is a disease that causes areas of bark or woody tissue to die, crack, and sink. It typically looks like a sunken, discoloured patch on a branch or trunk — darker than the surrounding healthy bark, sometimes oozing, sometimes cracked open.

Key things to understand:

  • It is caused by fungi or bacteria that infect the plant, usually entering through a wound or weak spot
  • The dead area slowly expands outward, killing more tissue as it grows
  • If a canker grows large enough to go all the way around a branch (called girdling), it cuts off the flow of water and nutrients — and that branch dies
  • Common trees affected include apples, pears, roses, and many forest trees

Gardeners dread canker because it can disfigure or kill an otherwise healthy plant if not caught and cut away early.

The word also applies to certain animal diseases, though it refers to somewhat different conditions depending on the animal:

  • In horses: Canker is a disease of the hoof. It causes the tissue in the underside of the hoof (especially the frog — the rubbery V-shaped pad) to become soft, spongy, and foul-smelling, essentially rotting from the inside. It's difficult to treat and painful for the horse.
  • In dogs and cats: "Ear canker" is an older, informal term for a chronic ear infection or inflammation — the kind that causes a dog to shake its head and scratch at its ear persistently. Modern veterinarians tend to say ear infection or otitis, but canker is still used in everyday speech.
  • In birds (especially pigeons and birds of prey): Canker refers to an infection caused by a tiny parasite (Trichomonas gallinae) that creates yellowish, cheesy-looking lesions inside the mouth and throat. It can spread quickly through a flock and be fatal if it blocks the bird's airway.

In literature, formal writing, and thoughtful speech, canker is used figuratively to describe anything that corrupts, erodes, or spreads destructively within something that was once healthy — the way a real canker eats into living tissue.

Examples of how it's used:

  • "Corruption is the canker of this institution."
  • "Greed became a canker that slowly destroyed their friendship."
  • "Hatred is a canker that spreads if left untreated."

When used this way, the speaker is drawing on the word's original power: this isn't just a problem — it's something alive, spreading, and gradually consuming from within. It implies that if nothing is done, the damage will grow. The metaphor is old and powerful, and you'll find it often in Shakespeare, the King James Bible, and classic literature.

Across all these uses, a canker shares these qualities:

  • It is a wound, sore, or area of decay
  • It occurs in something living — a body, a plant, an animal, a society
  • It tends to spread or worsen if unaddressed
  • It destroys from within, not from an obvious external blow

That's canker: not just damage, but the kind that quietly eats away.
2476: "Canned" has a few related meanings, all connected by a single core idea: something that was made in advance, stored, and is ready to be used at any time — rather than being freshly made right now.
Meaning 1: Food preserved in a sealed metal container

The most literal meaning. Canned food has been cooked, sealed inside a metal tin, and can be stored for months or years without going bad.

canned tomatoes, canned tuna, canned soup, canned corn

This is the straightforward, physical sense of the word — you've certainly seen canned goods in a store.
Meaning 2: Pre-made, pre-recorded, or standardized (the more important meaning)

This is where "canned" gets interesting and widely used. It describes something that was prepared in advance, stored like a can of food, and is now being pulled out and used repeatedly — rather than being created fresh, in the moment, for this specific situation.

The key ideas this meaning carries:

It's not original. It was made once and is reused many times, often with little or no adjustment.

It lacks authenticity. Because it wasn't created specifically for this moment or this person, it can feel hollow, impersonal, or mechanical.

It's convenient but not genuine. Like canned soup — quick and easy, but not as good as something freshly made.

The classic example: canned laughter

Have you ever watched an old TV sitcom and heard a laughing sound every time a joke was made? That's canned laughter — pre-recorded laughing sounds that were added to the show in editing. No one is actually laughing in the moment at your TV. The producers recorded laughter once, stored it, and inserted it into the show wherever they wanted. It sounds artificial precisely because it is.

Canned response / canned reply

If you contact a company's customer service and receive a reply that feels like it was written for everyone and not specifically for you — it probably was. That's a canned response: a template answer, pre-written, stored, and sent out automatically or copy-pasted whenever a similar question comes in. It solves the problem quickly but feels impersonal.

Canned speech / canned presentation

A politician who travels city to city delivering essentially the same speech to every audience is giving a canned speech. A salesperson who walks into every meeting and delivers the same pitch word-for-word is giving a canned presentation. There's nothing spontaneous or tailored about it.

Canned answer

If someone asks you a difficult question and you immediately launch into a smooth, well-rehearsed explanation without thinking — you gave a canned answer. You had it prepared and waiting. (This can be neutral or even positive — being prepared isn't always a bad thing — but it often implies the answer felt a little too polished, a little too ready.)
The tone and feeling of the word

"Canned" in this figurative sense is usually mildly negative or dismissive. When someone calls something "canned," they're typically criticizing it for lacking:

  • Spontaneity — it wasn't created in the moment
  • Sincerity — it doesn't feel like it came from a real, thoughtful place
  • Originality — it's the same thing being reused again and again
  • Personal relevance — it wasn't made for you specifically

Saying "that was a canned response" is essentially saying: "They didn't actually think about my situation. They just pulled out a ready-made reply."

However, in some contexts "canned" is used neutrally, especially in professional settings. "I have a canned answer for this question" simply means "I've answered this so many times that I have a well-prepared reply" — without necessarily implying anything dishonest or lazy.
Meaning 3: Fired from a job (informal slang)

In informal American English, "canned" can mean dismissed from employment — fired. Just as a factory seals something in a can and sends it away, a company "cans" an employee and sends them away.

"He got canned after missing three deadlines."
"She was canned without any warning."

This usage is casual and a bit dated, but you'll still encounter it, especially in American films, novels, and informal speech.

In very informal, mostly older British and American slang, "canned" can mean intoxicated.

"He showed up to the party completely canned."

This meaning is uncommon today — you're unlikely to hear it much in modern everyday speech — but it appears in older literature and films.

Most common and important → Pre-made, pre-recorded, lacking originality or spontaneity (canned laughter, canned response, canned speech)

Literal/everyday → Food preserved in a metal tin (canned beans, canned fruit)

Informal → Fired from a job (got canned)

Rare/dated slang → Drunk (completely canned)

All meanings of "canned" trace back to the same image: a can is something sealed, preserved, and stored — ready for later use, but no longer fresh. Whether it's food, laughter, or a speech, calling something "canned" means it's been packaged in advance and stored for reuse, rather than being made fresh for the moment at hand.
2477:
Cannibalism is the act of eating the flesh — and sometimes other body parts — of a member of one's own species.

In plain words: if a human eats another human, that is cannibalism. If a lion eats another lion, that is also cannibalism. The key condition is that the eater and the eaten belong to the same species.

The word describes the act or practice, not a single event. So:

  • One isolated incident = an act of cannibalism.
  • A repeated or culturally accepted practice = the practice of cannibalism.

Both uses are correct. The noun simply names the behavior.

This is the most well-known form. Historically, it has occurred across different parts of the world and under very different circumstances. It broadly falls into a few categories:

1. Survival cannibalism
When people are starving with no other food source, some have resorted to eating the dead. The most famous documented case is the Donner Party (1846–47), a group of American pioneers stranded in snow who ate those who had already died to survive. This is widely considered the most "understandable" form in moral terms, because it involves eating those already dead — not killing anyone.

2. Ritual or cultural cannibalism
Some ancient and tribal societies practiced cannibalism as part of religious or cultural rituals. It was sometimes believed that eating part of an enemy warrior's body — or even a respected elder — would transfer their strength, courage, or spirit to the eater. This is sometimes called endocannibalism (eating one's own group members, often as a funeral rite) or exocannibalism (eating outsiders or enemies).

3. Predatory or criminal cannibalism
This refers to cases where a person kills another specifically to eat them, outside of any cultural or survival context. This is the rarest form and is universally treated as a severe crime in modern societies.

Cannibalism is actually fairly common in the animal kingdom and is not considered morally wrong — it is simply a natural behavior. Examples:

  • Spiders: Female black widow spiders sometimes eat the male after mating.
  • Praying mantises: Similar behavior to spiders.
  • Fish: Many species eat their own eggs or young if resources are scarce.
  • Pigs, rats, bears, chimpanzees: All documented cases of cannibalism exist among these animals.

In nature, cannibalism often serves a purpose — eliminating competition, gaining nutrients, or removing weak offspring.

Technically, cannibalism refers to consuming the body of a member of one's own species. This most commonly means flesh (muscle tissue), but it can include organs, blood, or bone marrow. The word covers all of these.

However, in everyday speech and media, "flesh" is the most commonly implied element.

• Endocannibalism: Eating members of your own social group (family, tribe). Often ritualistic.
  • Exocannibalism: Eating members of an outside group (enemies, strangers). Often aggressive or symbolic.
  • Autophagy: Technically means "self-eating," but this word is used in biology to describe cells consuming their own damaged parts — it's a completely different concept and should not be confused with cannibalism.
  • Cannibal (noun): The person or creature who commits cannibalism.
  • Cannibalistic (adjective): Describing behavior that involves or resembles cannibalism. ("The tribe had cannibalistic rituals.")
  • Cannibalize (verb): Has an extended meaning in business — when one company's product reduces the sales of its own other product, that's called "cannibalizing" its own market. This is a metaphorical use, borrowed from the word's core meaning of consuming one's own kind.

In virtually every modern human society, cannibalism — especially the killing of another person for the purpose of eating them — is one of the strongest moral and legal taboos that exists. Even in historical cultures that practiced it, it was usually tightly regulated by ritual and context, not a free-for-all.

The revulsion most people feel toward cannibalism is thought to come from a combination of:

  • Deeply ingrained social norms about respect for the human body.
  • Fear of disease (eating human flesh can transmit serious neurological diseases like kuru, a fatal brain disorder).
  • The fundamental moral weight of treating a person as food.

Cannibalism = the act or practice of consuming the flesh (or body) of one's own species.

It applies to humans and animals alike. In humans, it has occurred in contexts ranging from desperate survival to ritual practice to criminal violence. In animals, it is a natural, observable behavior. In modern human society, it is almost universally condemned and illegal. The word also has a metaphorical extension in business and economics, where it describes a product or strategy that consumes its own company's resources or market share.
2478: A cannoli is a classic Italian pastry dessert — something you eat as a sweet treat, most famously from the island of Sicily in southern Italy. It has become one of the most recognized Italian desserts in the world, especially in places like the United States where Italian immigrants brought it along with their culture.

Picture a small, hollow, tube-shaped crispy shell — roughly the size and shape of a finger, or a thick cigar. That crunchy outer shell is stuffed, end to end, with a thick, soft, creamy filling that peeks out from both open ends. It looks a bit like a filled wafer roll or a crunchy cream-filled pipe.

A cannoli has exactly two essential components:

1. The shell
The outer crust is made from a simple pastry dough — flour, a bit of fat, sometimes a touch of wine or vinegar — that is rolled thin, wrapped around a small metal tube, and then deep-fried in hot oil. Frying is what gives it that signature crunch and a slightly bubbly, golden-brown surface. Once fried, the metal tube is slid out, leaving behind a perfectly hollow, crispy cylinder. This shell stays firm and crunchy on the outside.

2. The filling
The traditional filling is made primarily from ricotta cheese — a soft, mild, fresh Italian cheese with a slightly grainy texture. This ricotta is mixed with sugar to sweeten it and whipped to make it smooth and creamy. Sometimes a splash of vanilla or a tiny bit of cinnamon is added for flavor. The result is a lightly sweet, rich, fluffy cream that is piped into the hollow shell just before serving.

Cannoli are rarely plain. Common additions include:

  • Mini chocolate chips mixed into the filling or sprinkled on the exposed cream at both ends
  • Candied fruit peel (like orange or citron) folded into the filling or used as garnish at the tips
  • Crushed pistachios pressed onto the ends where the cream pokes out — this is very traditional
  • A dusting of powdered sugar over the whole thing

These touches add texture, color, and complementary flavors.
What makes it special: the contrast

The soul of a cannoli is the contrast between its two parts. You get a crisp, slightly savory, crackly shell on the outside and a cool, soft, sweet cream on the inside — all in one bite. This play between crunchy and creamy, between the neutral pastry and the sweet filling, is exactly what makes cannoli so satisfying and beloved.

Here is a small but useful thing to know: in Italian, one piece is called a cannolo, and more than one are called cannoli. However, in everyday English — especially in American English — people say "a cannoli" even when referring to just one. So you might hear "give me a cannoli" or "I ate two cannoli," and both are perfectly normal in English usage.

Cannoli are almost always filled to order at a bakery or pastry shop — meaning the shell is kept separate, and the cream is piped in right before you eat it. This is done on purpose: if the cream sits inside the shell for too long, the moisture soaks into the crispy dough and it goes soft and soggy. A freshly filled cannoli has a shell that snaps when you bite into it. A cannoli that has been sitting filled for hours will be disappointingly soft and limp. This is why people who know their cannoli always insist on eating them fresh.

They are typically eaten as a dessert after a meal, or as a standalone snack from a bakery. They come in different sizes — standard ones are about 9 to 15 cm (roughly 4 to 6 inches) long, and "mini cannoli" are bite-sized versions, popular at parties.

Over the years, bakers have gotten creative:

  • Chocolate shells — the dough is made with cocoa powder for a dark, chocolatey crust
  • Pistachio filling — ricotta is mixed with pistachio paste for a green, nutty cream
  • Mascarpone filling — mascarpone (a richer, buttery Italian cream cheese) is used instead of or alongside ricotta for an even creamier result
  • Flavored fillings — strawberry, lemon, hazelnut, and many other variations exist in modern bakeries

However, if someone says "cannoli" without any qualifier, they almost always mean the classic version: crispy fried shell + sweetened ricotta cream.

A cannoli is a crunchy, tube-shaped, deep-fried pastry shell packed with sweet, creamy ricotta filling — a dessert from Sicily, Italy, loved worldwide for its satisfying crunch-meets-cream contrast, often garnished with chocolate chips, candied fruit, or pistachios.
2479:
A cannonade is a long, heavy, and continuous burst of cannon fire — not just one shot, but many cannons firing again and again, repeatedly, over a stretch of time, creating a thunderous, relentless storm of destruction.

Think of it this way: if a single cannon shot is like one knock on a door, a cannonade is like someone hammering that door without stopping — boom, boom, boom, boom — for minutes or even hours.

The most important thing to understand is that a cannonade has three qualities working together:

1. It involves cannons or heavy artillery.
A cannonade is specifically tied to large, powerful weapons — cannons, artillery guns, that sort of thing. It is not used for small gunfire like pistols or rifles.

2. It is sustained and continuous.
This is the heart of the word. A cannonade does not stop after one or two shots. It keeps going. Cannons are loaded, fired, reloaded, and fired again — over and over. The attack is relentless. This is what separates a cannonade from a simple "shot" or even a "volley" (which is one quick, simultaneous burst from multiple weapons and then it's done). A cannonade pounds a target over time.

3. It is heavy and intense.
A cannonade is not a light or scattered exchange of fire. It is overwhelming in its scale and power. It typically involves multiple cannons all firing together, creating a wall of destruction. The noise alone would be deafening — the ground would shake, smoke would blacken the air, and anyone nearby would feel the percussion in their chest.

Imagine a medieval or early modern battlefield. Two armies face each other. Before the infantry soldiers even march forward to fight, the generals order their cannons to fire — not once, but relentlessly — to weaken the enemy's defenses, break their formations, and terrify them. Cannonballs tear through the air for minutes, sometimes hours. That sustained, punishing artillery attack is a cannonade.

One of history's most famous examples is the cannonade at Gettysburg during the American Civil War (July 3, 1863). Before the ill-fated "Pickett's Charge," Confederate forces unleashed a massive cannonade — roughly 150 cannons firing continuously for nearly two hours — against Union positions. It was meant to soften the Union lines before the infantry assault. Witnesses described it as the most terrifying sound they had ever heard in their lives.
How It Differs from Similar Words

It is easy to mix this word up with others, so here is a clear distinction:

  • Shot — a single projectile fired from a single weapon. One moment. One impact.
  • Volley — multiple weapons firing at the same time, all at once, but briefly.
  • Bombardment — a broad, general term for any sustained attack using heavy weapons (bombs, missiles, artillery). It's bigger and more general in scope.
  • Cannonade — specifically a sustained and continuous discharge of cannons or artillery. It sits in that precise space: heavier than a volley, more specific than a bombardment, far beyond a single shot.

Like many powerful words, cannonade has also broken free from the battlefield and entered everyday language as a metaphor. People use it to describe any overwhelming, relentless outpouring of something.

For example:

  • "The politician faced a cannonade of criticism from the press."
  • "The teacher unleashed a cannonade of questions on the unprepared students."
  • "The comedian received a cannonade of laughter from the audience."

In each case, the idea is the same: something coming at you hard, fast, and without letting up — just like real cannon fire. The figurative use works precisely because of the word's literal meaning: relentless, heavy, overwhelming.

Words carry atmosphere, and cannonade carries a lot of it. It is a word that feels loud, powerful, and dramatic. When you read or hear it, you are meant to feel the scale and intensity of what is being described. It is not a gentle word. It does not suggest a small or brief event. It suggests something that dominates an entire scene — something you cannot escape, cannot ignore, and cannot easily survive.

A cannonade (noun) = a prolonged, heavy, and continuous discharge of cannon or artillery fire, involving multiple weapons firing repeatedly over time, creating an overwhelming and relentless attack. It can also be used figuratively to describe any intense, sustained outpouring — of criticism, noise, questions, or any force that hits you repeatedly and powerfully without pause.
2480:
Imagine someone who is not just smart, but smart in a very practical, grounded way — someone who reads situations accurately, makes careful decisions, and is almost never fooled or caught off guard. That is the essence of canny.

A canny person combines sharp judgment with caution. They don't just think fast — they think well. They know when to act, when to wait, and how to get the best out of a situation without making careless mistakes.
Breaking It Down: What "Canny" Actually Means

Think of "canny" as having two elements working together:

1. Sharpness — A canny person sees what others miss. They notice the small details, spot the hidden catch in a deal, or sense when something is off. This is real-world intelligence — the kind that comes from experience and keen observation, not just from reading books.

2. Careful caution — A canny person doesn't charge ahead recklessly. They are deliberate and measured. Before making a move, they've already thought about what could go wrong.

Together, these two qualities describe someone who is hard to fool, hard to beat, and rarely makes avoidable mistakes.

"Canny" is almost always a positive or admiring word. When you call someone canny, you are giving them a compliment — you're saying they have a kind of quiet, solid wisdom. There's a sense of respect in the word.

However, it carries a very subtle edge of calculation — a canny person is smart in a way that is useful to themselves. They look out for their own interests wisely. This is not a negative thing, but it does separate "canny" from a word like "kind" or "generous." A canny person is smart, not necessarily warm.

You will most often hear "canny" used in the context of money, business, or strategy — situations where careful thinking and smart judgment lead to better outcomes.

  • "She was a canny investor who bought property before prices rose."
    She made a smart, carefully judged financial move.
  • "The canny politician knew exactly when to speak and when to stay quiet."
    He read the situation well and acted shrewdly.
  • "It was a canny decision to wait before making an offer."
    The decision showed practical wisdom and good timing.
  • "He's a canny negotiator — you won't get a bad deal past him."
    He is sharp-eyed and careful; he won't be outsmarted.

These words are close to "canny" in meaning, but each has its own flavour:

  • Shrewd — Very similar to canny. But "shrewd" can sometimes suggest someone who is a little more calculating or cold. "Canny" feels slightly warmer and more earthy.
  • Astute — Means perceptive and intelligent, but it leans more toward mental sharpness and is more formal. "Astute" fits an intellectual; "canny" fits a wise, experienced person who has learned from life.
  • Cunning — This is where things get important. Cunning implies cleverness used for deception or manipulation. A cunning person tricks others. A canny person outsmarts others without necessarily being dishonest. "Canny" is mostly positive; "cunning" is mostly negative.
  • Clever — More general. "Clever" just means mentally quick. "Canny" is more specific — it means practically wise, experienced, and careful.
  • Savvy — Very close to canny in feel. "Savvy" is more informal and modern; "canny" is slightly more traditional and is more common in British English.
What a Canny Person Is NOT

To sharpen your understanding further, here is what "canny" does not mean:

  • A canny person is not reckless — they always think before acting.
  • A canny person is not naïve or gullible — they are not easily deceived.
  • A canny person is not dishonest — being canny doesn't require lying or cheating (that would be cunning).
  • A canny person is not just "book smart" — canny is about real-world judgment, not academic intelligence.
A Special Regional Meaning (Scottish and Northern English)

In Scotland and parts of Northern England, "canny" has an additional, quite different meaning in everyday speech. There, it can simply mean nice, pleasant, or gentle — as in "He's a canny lad" (He's a nice guy) or "That's a canny idea" (That's a good idea). In some cases, it can also mean careful or gentle in a soft, considerate sense — "Go canny" meaning "Go carefully" or "Take it easy."

This regional meaning is warm and affectionate, quite unlike the shrewdness of the standard meaning. If you see "canny" in Scottish writing or dialogue, the context will usually make it clear which meaning is being used.

Canny means shrewdly clever and carefully practical — describing a person who makes smart, well-judged decisions, sees situations clearly, and is very hard to fool or outmanoeuvre, especially in matters of money or strategy.
2481:
At the heart of every meaning of "canon" is one central idea: something officially recognized and accepted as true, legitimate, or authoritative. Think of it as the "official, approved version" of something. Everything else — outside the canon — is unofficial, questionable, or rejected.

With that core in mind, here are all the major meanings:
1. In Religion — The Official Holy Texts & Church Rules

This is the oldest use of the word. A canon in religion refers to the official list of books accepted as genuine and sacred scripture. For example, the "Biblical canon" is the agreed-upon collection of books that make up the Bible. Not every ancient religious text made it in — church authorities debated which books were truly holy and which were not. The ones that "made it" became the canon.

A canon can also mean an official rule or law of a church. This is where the phrase "canon law" comes from — the body of laws that governs a religious institution, especially the Roman Catholic Church.
2. In Literature and Art — The "Great Works"

In the world of books, art, and culture, the canon means the body of works considered most important, foundational, and worth studying. The "Western literary canon," for example, includes writers like Shakespeare, Homer, and Dante — authors widely regarded as essential to understanding literature.

The word also applies to a single author. An author's canon is the complete set of works genuinely and officially attributed to them. Shakespeare's canon includes all the plays and poems scholars agree he actually wrote. Works of disputed authorship fall outside the canon.

So the literary canon is essentially: the official list of what matters most.

This is the most widely used meaning today, especially in conversations about movies, TV shows, books, comics, and video games.

In fiction, canon means the officially established facts, events, and details of a story's universe — everything that "really happened" according to the creators.

For example: In the Harry Potter universe, what J.K. Rowling wrote in the novels is canon — it truly happened in that world. If a fan writes their own story where Hermione becomes a Slytherin, that is "fan fiction" — it is not canon. The author didn't say it happened.

When someone asks "Is that canon?" they are asking: Did the official creators establish this as a real, confirmed fact in the story's world?

The opposite of canon in this context is called non-canon — anything unofficial, unconfirmed, or contradicted by the creators.

One important nuance: a story can have multiple layers of canon. For instance, in the Star Wars universe, Disney has declared that only the films, Disney+ shows, and approved books are "canon." Older novels and stories from before Disney's takeover were officially labeled "non-canon" (they call it "Legends"). This shows that canon can be redefined by whoever holds authority over a story.
4. In Music — A Type of Composition

In music, a canon is a specific compositional technique where one voice or instrument plays a melody, and then another voice begins playing that same melody slightly later, overlapping with the first. The voices essentially "chase" each other, creating a layered, interwoven sound.

The most famous example is Pachelbel's Canon in D. A simpler everyday example is singing "Row, Row, Row Your Boat" in overlapping groups — one group starts, then another group starts the same song from the beginning while the first group is still singing. That overlapping technique is the essence of a musical canon.
5. As a General Principle — An Accepted Rule or Standard

More broadly, "canon" can simply mean an accepted rule, principle, or criterion in any field. For example: "The canons of good journalism include accuracy, fairness, and verification." Here, "canons" just means the established, widely agreed-upon standards that define what good practice looks like in that profession.

Every meaning of "canon" returns to the same root idea: official recognition by an authority. Whether it's:

  • the officially accepted books of the Bible,
  • the officially great works of literature,
  • the officially confirmed facts of a fictional universe,
  • the strict rule-based structure of a musical form, or
  • the officially accepted standards of a profession —

...a canon is always about what has been formally recognized, agreed upon, and accepted as legitimate by whoever holds the relevant authority. Anything outside that boundary is unofficial, disputed, or simply not part of the canon.
2482:
Canonical means officially accepted, standard, and authoritative. When something is called canonical, it means it has been recognized — by experts, institutions, tradition, or the appropriate authority — as the genuine, correct, or definitive version of something.

Think of it this way: if you had a big important question, and you needed the answer — not just any answer, but the one that everyone trusted and agreed on — that answer would be the canonical one.
Breaking It Down in Different Contexts

The word "canonical" is used across many different fields, and while it always carries the same core meaning, its flavor shifts slightly depending on the context. Here's how it works in each one.

1. In Religion
